questions.question: 1. Metals react with air, water and dilute acids in different ways. A. Describe how magnesium reacts with oxygen? (2 marks). B. Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (2 marks). C. Which is more reactive magnesium and zinc? (1 mark). 2. Look at the table below, then compare how they react with hydrochloric acid. The first one is done for you. (4 marks). Metal / React with hydrochloric acid: Lead - Very slow; Magnesium - ; Zinc - ; Iron - ; Gold - . 3. Graph X and graph Y concerns about concentration. A. Which graph has more concentration? (1 mark). B. Which graph contains less concentration? (1 mark). C. Which curve did the reaction come completion first? (1 mark). 4. Complete the paragraph using the words below. (5 marks). Words: Faster, Collisions, Succeed, Collision theory, Effective collision. ............ refers that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the number of collisions of reactant particles. The more number of ............ of reactant particles, the more they react with one another and thus the ............ the rate of a reaction. However not all collisions ............ in producing a reaction. Collisions that succeed in producing a reaction are called ............ .

questions.answer_guide: 1.A. Magnesium burns in oxygen (air) with a bright white flame, forming a white powder of magnesium oxide. B. 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). C. Magnesium is more reactive than zinc. 2. See matching pairs: Magnesium reacts very fast/vigorously; zinc fairly fast; iron slowly; gold does not react (lead given as very slow). 3.A. X (it has the faster rate, so the more concentrated solution). B. Y. C. X (its curve levels off first). 4. Collision theory; Collisions; Faster; Succeed; Effective collision.

Oxygen 1s² 2s² 2p⁴: [↑↓] [↑↓] [↑↓][↑][↑]. 2.A. Group 3 (13): aluminium has electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹, so 3 electrons in its outer shell. B. questions.section: PART TWO: STRUCTURED QUESTIONS (85 MARKS) - QUESTION THREE: ENERGY IN CHEMISTRY (13 MARKS)
questions.question: 1. The standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethene is -1411 kJ/mol. A. Define enthalpy change of combustion. (2 marks). B. Write a balanced equation for the reaction including state symbols. (3 marks). C. Draw the energy profile diagram for the combustion of ethene. (3 marks). D. Draw the displayed formula of ethene. (2 marks). 2. Standard enthalpy change for a reaction takes place under 3 standard conditions. A. Write the 3 standard conditions needed for the reaction to take place. (3 marks).
questions.answer_guide: 1.A. Enthalpy change of combustion is the heat energy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen under standard conditions. B. C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)  ΔH = -1411 kJ/mol. C. Exothermic energy profile: vertical axis energy, horizontal axis progress of reaction; reactants (C₂H₄ + 3O₂) at a higher level, products (2CO₂ + 2H₂O) at a lower level, a downward arrow labelled ΔH = -1411 kJ/mol, optionally with a hump for the activation energy. D. Displayed formula of ethene: H₂C=CH₂ drawn with each carbon bonded to two H atoms and a C=C double bond between the carbons (H–C(=C)–H pattern: each C has two H). 2.A. Temperature of 298 K (25 °C); pressure of 100 kPa (1 atm); concentration of 1 mol/dm³ for solutions (with all substances in their standard states).

questions.section: PART TWO: STRUCTURED QUESTIONS (85 MARKS) - QUESTION FOUR: MOLE AND STOICHIOMETRY (16 MARKS)
questions.question: 1. Determine the relative molecular mass of the following: a) Copper carbonate CuCO₃ (Cu = 64, C = 12, O = 16) (3 marks). b) Lead(II) nitrate Pb(NO₃)₂ (Pb = 207, N = 14, O = 16) (3 marks). 2. In a chemical reaction sodium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid. Here is a balanced equation for the reaction. Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). a) How many moles of hydrochloric acid react with one mole of sodium carbonate? (1 mark). b) How many moles of sodium chloride are formed in the reaction? (1 mark). c) How many moles of carbon dioxide are produced in the reaction? (1 mark). d) Calculate the relative molecular mass of sodium chloride NaCl. (2 marks). 3. 1.843 g of an organic compound M containing hydrogen, carbon, oxygen and Sulphur, on combustion gave 3.08 g of carbon dioxide and 0.63 g of water. In a separate experiment, the same mass of M gave 2.7013 g of barium sulphate when the sulphur in the compound was converted to barium sulphate. a) Determine the empirical formula of M. b) If the molecular mass of M is 158, determine the molecular formula of M. (5 marks).
questions.answer_guide: 1.a) Mr(CuCO₃) = 64 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 124. b) Mr(Pb(NO₃)₂) = 207 + 2 × (14 + 3 × 16) = 207 + 124 = 331. 2.a) 2 moles. b) 2 moles. c) 1 mole. d) Mr(NaCl) = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5). 3. Carbon: 3.08 / 44 = 0.07 mol CO₂ → 0.07 mol C (0.84 g). Hydrogen: 0.63 / 18 = 0.035 mol H₂O → 0.07 mol H (0.07 g). Sulphur: 2.7013 / 233 = 0.0116 mol BaSO₄ → 0.0116 mol S (0.371 g). Oxygen by difference: 1.843 - 0.84 - 0.07 - 0.371 = 0.562 g → 0.035 mol O. Mole ratio C : H : S : O = 0.07 : 0.07 : 0.0116 : 0.035 = 6 : 6 : 1 : 3. a) Empirical formula = C₆H₆O₃S (Mr = 158). b) Molecular mass 158 / empirical mass 158 = 1, so the molecular formula is C₆H₆O₃S.

questions.answer_guide: 1.A. See matching pairs (the 5 ions to complete: OH⁻, NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻). 2. Draw a dotted line from the δ+ hydrogen of a water molecule to the lone pair on the nitrogen of ammonia (N···H–O); a bond from a δ+ H of ammonia to the oxygen of water is also possible. A. H₂O: 2 lone pairs and 2 bonding pairs. NH₃: 1 lone pair and 3 bonding pairs. B. London dispersion forces (van der Waals forces); dipole-dipole forces; hydrogen bonding. C. Weak: a hydrogen bond is much weaker than a covalent or ionic bond, although it is the strongest of the intermolecular forces.

questions.answer_guide: 1.a. Pentane. b. Butanal. c. 3-methylhexan-3-ol. d. 2-methylhexane (check the chain length against the original figure). e. Propanone (acetone). 2.a. Addition reaction: a reaction in which two or more molecules combine to form a single product, usually when atoms add across the C=C or C≡C bond of an unsaturated compound. b. Substitution reaction: a reaction in which an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms. c. Aliphatic hydrocarbons: hydrocarbons whose carbon atoms are joined in straight chains, branched chains or non-aromatic rings (they contain no benzene ring). 3. Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
